citations.narrative:
During the inspection, APHIS Officials observed two wild felids (one caracal and one serval) on the premises. Acquisition
records indicate that they were obtained in March 2025. The applicant verbally confirmed that the serval has been
exhibited since acquisition. However, the facility's current license does not authorize the exhibition of wild felids.
Licenses must specifically authorize the use of each of the following groups of animals: Group 5 (baboons and
nonbrachiating species larger than 33 lbs.) and Group 6 (great apes over 55 lbs. and brachiating species) nonhuman
primates; exotic and wild felids (including but not limited to lions, tigers, leopards, cheetahs, jaguars, cougars, lynx,
servals, bobcats, and caracals, and any hybrid cross thereof); hyenas and/or exotic and wild canids (including but not
limited to wolves, coyotes, foxes, and jackals); bears; and mega-herbivores (including but not limited to elephants,
rhinoceroses, hippopotamuses, and giraffes). The licensee must obtain a new license authorizing these animal groups
before exhibiting any animal that is beyond the types or numbers authorized under the existing license.

The unopened bags of bedding used for the non-human primate enclosures is being stored directly on the floor inside the
housing facility. Supplies of food and bedding must be stored in a manner that protects the supplies from spoilage,
contamination, and vermin infestation. The supplies must be stored off the floor and away from the walls, to allow cleaning
underneath and around the supplies. Only the food and bedding currently being used may be kept in animal areas, and
when not in actual use, open food and bedding supplies must be kept in leakproof containers with tightly fitting lids to
prevent spoilage and contamination.

The outdoor enclosure housing two coatis is less than three feet away from the facility’s perimeter fence. During this
inspection, one side of the coati habitat structure measured approximately 2 feet and 2 inches from the perimeter fence.
Having a perimeter fence in place protects the animals in the facility by restricting animals and unauthorized persons from
going through it or under it, permitting contact with the animals in the facility by unauthorized animals or patrons visiting
the facility. Additionally, it serves as a secondary containment system for the animals in the facility. The perimeter fence
must be of sufficient distance from the outside of the primary enclosure to prevent physical contact between animals
inside the enclosure and animals or persons outside the perimeter fence. Non-dangerous animals housed in outdoor
facilities require a 6-foot-tall perimeter fence around their enclosure and must be at least 3-feet away from any enclosures
or buildings, unless an approved variance has been issued in writing by the Administrator.
This is a 1st Re-License Inspection for a Class “C” license. The inspection and exit briefing were conducted with the
applicant.
All items must be in compliance within 2 more inspections or by 03 October 2026 or the applicant will forfeit the license
fee and must wait 6 months to reapply. Please contact your inspector to schedule your next Re-License Inspection.
Regulated activity can continue under your existing USDA license until it expires.
Additional Inspectors:
Makayla Willis, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
